speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.30 pm.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In the past, cigarette smoking and drug abuse were two separate issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: People are using vaporisers to abuse etomidate or even other more serious controlled drugs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This makes vaporisers a bridge between these two worlds, creating new challenges in vaping enforcement and health protection.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Hence, the Ministry of Health (MOH) worked closely with the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) and other agencies to leverage existing legislation to develop a new regime for enforcement, rehabilitation and education.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Specifically, as our existing laws, particularly the Tobacco (Control of Advertisements and Sale) Act and Poisons Act, are not designed for such enforcement actions, we temporarily listed etomidate and its analogues as Class C controlled drugs in the Misuse of Drugs Act (MDA).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I will refer to these substances collectively as “etomidate”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We then used legislative levers in the Poisons Act to take action against first-time etomidate vaporiser offenders as well as repeat offenders under the MDA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It was not ideal, but we made it work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In gist, this is how the enforcement system works today, since September 2025.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: First, we imposed much tougher penalties for those who illegally import, sell, supply or traffic etomidate – enabled by listing etomidate as a controlled drug under the MDA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Second, we created a rapid escalation of actions against etomidate vaporiser users.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: First-time offenders are required to attend rehabilitation, in lieu of prosecution for illegal possession of etomidate under the Poisons Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Those who default on the rehabilitation are prosecuted under the Poisons Act and may be subject to a custodial sentence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Third, repeat etomidate vaporiser offenders are placed under mandatory urine-test supervision, or detained in the Drug Rehabilitation Centre (DRC), under the MDA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Among the offenders placed on rehabilitation, 42 defaulted their rehabilitation – of which one has been convicted and imprisoned and the rest will be charged.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Seventy offenders have completed their rehabilitation programmes, with four youth offenders re-offending after their completion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The new law is built upon the existing Tobacco (Control of Advertisements and Sale) Act, which will be broadened and strengthened.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: First, we are renaming the Tobacco (Control of Advertisements and Sale) Act to the Tobacco and Vaporisers Control Act (TVCA).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This reflects the broader mandate and coverage of the new law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Second, we have updated the categories of prohibited products under the TVCA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: One, tobacco products, such as cigarettes, that contain any prescribed substances, or contain or emit substances exceeding prescribed limits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For example, this includes cigarettes whose emissions contain nicotine or tar in excess of the prescribed limits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The TVCA calls these "section 14 tobacco products".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Two, various types of prohibited tobacco products such as smokeless tobacco and heated tobacco products, and their components too.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The TVCA calls these "section 15 tobacco products".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And four, other imitation tobacco products that are not already covered by the other sections I mentioned above, and their components.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This allows us to future-proof our legislation, ensuring that new products that resemble any existing tobacco product or may be used to mimic the act of smoking, will be prohibited.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Future-proofing is important, especially given that the tobacco industry has been introducing new products to circumvent tobacco control regulations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: One example is products containing nicotine analogues, which will be considered a tobacco product moving forward, and can be prohibited under the TVCA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To be clear, products in all four categories are already prohibited currently under the Tobacco (Control of Advertisements and Sale) Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: When I say “prohibited”, I am referring to the entire supply ecosystem.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Hence, under the Bill, we are making it clear that giving, transporting, sending or delivering these prohibited products within Singapore, offering to do any of these acts and possessing such products for the purpose of doing any of these acts, are prohibited.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Third, in addition to the four categories, “Specified Psychoactive Substances” (SPS) will also come under the scope of the TVCA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These are substances or products that will be specified in a new Schedule, provided for in clause 23, being substances and products that can cause a psychoactive effect when consumed, and are also abused or likely to be abused by using a tobacco product, vaporiser or imitation tobacco product.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Etomidate, currently under the MDA, will be listed in this new Schedule.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Concurrently, etomidate will be removed from the MDA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Minister for Health can amend this Schedule by order in the Gazette.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The TVCA introduces two presumptions to do with the nature of SPS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The person does not need to know the name or chemical composition of the SPS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These provisions mirror sections 22A and 22B of the MDA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Fourth, we are consolidating the enforcement levers under various pieces of legislation today, under the TVCA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The offences and penalties for importing, supplying or abusing SPS products are similar to those in the MDA, to ensure similar level of deterrence.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Members may also access these materials through the MP@SGPARL App.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On the offence of consuming SPS, I would also like to highlight that although one of the Ministry of Health’s (MOH’s) criteria for listing a substance or product as an SPS is that it is abused or is likely to be abused by using a tobacco product, vaporiser or imitation tobacco product, the consumption offence is not confined to a specific mode.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This means that once a substance or product is listed as an SPS, even if an individual abuses the SPS through means other than a vaporiser, tobacco product or imitation tobacco product, for example, in its liquid form or through a patch, they can still be dealt with under the TVCA.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Like the MDA, it will be an offence for Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents to consume SPS overseas.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This deters locals from going abroad to feed their addiction to evade enforcement in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We have also introduced new offences to better protect our young people and children, again drawing from the MDA.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Section 19G targets adults who, being in possession of SPS products, first, knowingly or recklessly leave them where children can access them, or second, do not take reasonable steps to prevent the use of SPS products by young persons.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These adults are liable to imprisonment for up to 10 years for the first offence and imprisonment for two to 10 years for repeat offences.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Section 19H addresses adults who involve young or vulnerable persons in importing or supplying SPS products.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These adults are liable to imprisonment for four to 20 years and four to 15 strokes of the cane.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Section 19I makes it an offence to arrange or plan gatherings where SPS products are used or supplied.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Those found guilty are liable to imprisonment for two to 10 years and up to five strokes of the cane.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Today, this is effected in lieu of prosecution under Poisons Act.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will now provide for specific powers for the Chief Executive of the Health Sciences Authority (HSA) to order community-based rehabilitation and institutional treatment and rehabilitation under the TVCA.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: A community-based rehabilitation order can be made as long as the Chief Executive has grounds to believe that an individual has consumed an SPS.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Such grounds of belief could arise from, for example, observation of an individual behaving erratically or appearing disoriented who is also found in possession of an SPS product; or an individual testing positive for SPS in their urine or hair; or admission by an individual that they have consumed SPS.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Aside from SPS consumption, community-based rehabilitation can also be ordered for individuals who use vaporisers or section 15 tobacco products, based on observation of use, say, by an enforcement officer, or an admission of use.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As per our current practice, rehabilitation will only be ordered for repeat offenders, to support them to quit vaping.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Chief Executive can also require individuals subject to community-based rehabilitation orders to comply with other requirements, like undergoing urine or hair tests.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Besides community-based rehabilitation at the Institute of Mental Health and social service agencies, the Chief Executive can also, under section 19U, order institutional treatment and rehabilitation in the DRC, for re-offending cases of SPS consumption.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Chief Executive can also require certain persons, such as those discharged from DRC after treatment and rehabilitation for SPS consumption, to provide urine or hair samples to check if they are still consuming SPS.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Those who do not comply can be prosecuted.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We are therefore significantly increasing the penalties for offences involving these products to strengthen deterrence.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The enhanced penalties are coupled with the new powers to order rehabilitation, so that those who need help to quit can receive support.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For offences involving the import of vaporisers or section 15 tobacco products, we are introducing mandatory imprisonment for up to nine years, and additionally, offenders may face a fine of up to $300,000.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For offences involving the sale or supply, including possession for the purpose of sale or supply, of these products, offenders will face mandatory imprisonment for up to six years, and additionally, may face a fine of up to $200,000.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For offences involving the sale, supply or import of imitation tobacco products, the penalties will be increased to a fine of up to $100,000, or imprisonment of up to three years, or both for first-time offences; and a fine of up to $200,000, or imprisonment for up to six years, or both for repeat offences.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will also be introducing new statutory presumptions and offences to further strengthen our controls and enforcement on the supply chain.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Rebuttable presumptions relating to possession and knowledge of the nature of prohibited products under the new sections 14 to 16A and SPS products will be introduced, along with similar presumptions in relation to vehicles and trailers in which such products are found.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This will address the current challenge where most of the illegal operations bringing vaporisers and other prohibited products into Singapore are run from overseas, and it is extremely difficult for our enforcement authorities to obtain the evidence needed to prove that the suspect knew about the presence of the products found in their vehicles.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Similar presumption clauses are also found in the MDA.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: HSA has uncovered several cases of illegal vaporiser operations in warehouses and storage units.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These are often cases where offenders rented storage units to run their illegal operations.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To avoid liability, the owner or occupier must have exercised due care to prevent such storage from happening.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This may involve: conducting proper background checks on tenants, including asking them for uses of their storage spaces; explicit clauses in tenancy agreements on prohibited activities; conducting ad hoc inspections and so on.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: HSA will publish a handbook of best practices that owners and occupiers can refer to.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The intent is to allow us to take action against owners or occupiers who allow or turn a blind eye towards storage of such illegal products in their premises for supply and distribution purposes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: While vaping is prohibited, some continue to do so in public settings, for example in night clubs, bars and pubs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Under clause 12, we are imposing obligations on owners and occupiers of specified premises to take certain actions when they find someone in possession of or using any section 15 tobacco product, vaporiser or imitation tobacco product.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Smoking (Prohibition in Certain Places) Act imposes similar obligations.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The TVCA will spell out the steps which owners and occupiers of specified premises will be required to carry out, such as telling the offending individual to stop or leave the premises and seeking HSA's assistance if necessary.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As a start, specified premises will include discotheques, pubs, bars, lounges and night clubs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These are entertainment venues where people often gather and where we have seen vaping incidents occur.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: HSA has already been working with some of these operators on anti-vaping measures in their premises, like putting up anti-vaping signages, and we are thankful for their cooperation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: HSA will continue to work closely with the operators to comply with this new requirement, creating a safer environment for patrons.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There are several related and consequential amendments to several other pieces of legislation, such as the Poisons Act, MDA, Civil Defence Act, Merchant Shipping Act, and Road Traffic Act, to align to the TVCA.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It consolidates the lessons we have learned over the last six months.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: With this Bill, we will move from temporary measures into a more structured approach, embedded in our legal framework, that can address current challenges and provides flexibility to respond to future trends.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I urge Members of the House to support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It was marketed as a non-addictive substitute for morphine and as a remedy for coughs, even for children.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Few imagined then that what was promoted as relief would soon become synonymous with addiction.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By the time governments recognised the harm, dependency had already entered homes across continents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The tragedy was not that society refused to act.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Today, it does not come in glass bottles.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It comes in sleek vaporisers and small pods designed to resemble pens and highlighters.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For many residents in our estates, this is no longer abstract.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Neighbours are raising complaints about vaping in void decks and playgrounds.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But residents will judge it not by how severe its penalties are, but by whether it truly protects families and restores confidence on the ground.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As the Deputy Chair of the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) for Health, I believe we must ensure that this legislation is not only tough, but properly calibrated, proportionate and effective in practice.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, are we protecting our youths in a way that is firm, fair and effective?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As a father of five children, I do not approach this as an abstract policy issue.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I ask whether the system will respond proportionately if a young person makes a mistake.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, while the Bill speaks of treatment and rehabilitation, we must balance deterrence against vaporiser use, which disproportionately appeals to youths, with offences now benchmarked against the MDA.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are we calibrating this appropriately for a problem that may involve young offenders who may not know or fully appreciate what they are consuming?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill introduces presumptions of possession and knowledge.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What charging guidance will distinguish deliberate abuse from peer pressure or deception?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will discretion be exercised for first-time cases?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While deterrence is important, we must ask whether mandatory imprisonment for young offenders may be counterproductive.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will custodial sentences reduce long-term harm, or entrench it?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What percentage reduction in youth cases is targeted within 12 to 24 months?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will reductions in school incidents and hospital presentations be publicly reported?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What is the projected impact on DRC capacity?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will youths caught with psychoactive vapes be segregated from hardened drug offenders?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must also consider the long-term consequences of convictions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will offences under this Act be treated as spent after a period?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If not, how will criminal records affect education, employment and reintegration?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If rehabilitation is our aim, youthful mistakes should not become lifelong barriers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill also empowers urine, hair and oral fluid testing, with presumptions triggered upon positive results.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What safeguards ensure laboratory accuracy and prevent wrongful penalisation?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Do we have the scientific capacity to detect emerging analogues quickly?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Speaker, Sir, will residents see real change in their daily lives?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we deter effectively without disproportionately burdening vulnerable youths?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A $10,000 fine may well be a manageable business expense for a lucrative syndicate.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For a vulnerable youth, it can be life altering.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must distinguish between masterminds who profit and runners who were coerced or misled.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill also expands enforcement powers to search persons, seize vehicles and seize cash.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What safeguards ensure proportional use of these powers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Agencies prioritise syndicates, but residents see daily offences.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will other ground agencies such as the National Environment Agency (NEA), Land Transport Authority (LTA), Town Councils or NParks and so on be empowered to act against blatant vaping offences so enforcement is not overly centralised?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On responsible persons, specified premises initially include public entertainment outlets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will we be outsourcing enforcement to managing agents and security guards in condominiums?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If so, will they understand their limits and obligations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is notifying authorities sufficient or must responsible persons retain offenders?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will clear standard operational procedures (SOPs) and training be issued?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill also introduces liability for owners who allow storage without due diligence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will clear guidance and safe harbour frameworks be provided?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Strong laws must translate into visible confidence on the ground.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, are we staying ahead of the market?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What is the timeline from detection to scheduling?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will structured horizon scanning and digital monitoring be institutionalised?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We cannot fight a fast-moving market with slow-moving processes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On upstream disruption, are we moving beyond intelligence sharing to coordinated operations targeting production hubs?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill also amends the Civil Defence Act, Merchant Shipping Act and Road Traffic Act, expanding liability for individuals under the influence of SPS.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are frontline officers trained to detect SPS impairment?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Unless we disrupt supply at its source, enforcement becomes cyclical.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By the time society realised the cost, addiction had taken root.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But there is a difference between then and now.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this debate, I have asked three essential questions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The device in a schoolbag does not have to become this generation's cough syrup.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And as a father, I take that responsibility to heart.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With that resolve, Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Bill notably increases the fine amounts for vape users, sellers and smugglers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While this is welcomed, given the proliferation of etomidate-laced vapes or "Kpods", I hope that enforcement efforts will provide users the opportunity to turn over a new leaf instead of inadvertently stigmatising them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is especially pertinent as vaping is prevalent mainly amongst children and teens who have a long future ahead of them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The recent popularity of Kpods too has further added to the risk that our children are exposed to.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is especially so as our brains continue to develop way into our mid-20s and vape use is especially harmful to the prefrontal cortex.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This means that the brain's neurocircuits end up being dysregulated.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: That is detrimental to attention, impulse control and mood.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Vape and nicotine use is associated with dependence, mental health problems and use of other addictive substances.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is why even though enforcement checks in school to stamp out such behaviour are welcome, we must also be cautious about being overly punitive with our approach to prevent students from being unduly stigmatised.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Instead, the focus has to be on giving them the opportunity and support to change.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For instance, expelling or suspending a student might set them back academically, especially if they are already lagging behind their peers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Because vape and nicotine use is ultimately addictive and causes brain changes, it should be treated as a chronic relapsing disease that may require multiple quit attempts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, I hope that the Government exercises understanding to its victims and abusers of vapes, whose lives and livelihoods are upended.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A 2012 study highlighted a lower socio-economic status and associating education level was associated with a higher prevalence of smoking and nicotine addiction.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Although it seems unrelated at first glance, our efforts to stamp out vaping can be a socio-economic one.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We can do so by ameliorating the undercurrents of inequality in our society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Aside from socio-economic factors, we should also aim to tackle or at least mitigate the psychological vicious circle that connects vaping and poor mental health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A New Zealand study found that people who did not smoke or vape were 40% more likely to do so if they are experiencing mental distress.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, vaping does not provide the path of least resistance for someone who wishes to escape their circumstances.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In fact, nicotine and vapes is associated with increased stress and anxiety.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Vape users are also more likely to attempt suicide compared to non-users.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This ultimately causes a vicious feedback loop that cycles users between poor mental health, vaping and back again.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Although addressing mental health issues is targeted at a broader group, it has a knock-on effect of reducing the likelihood of people turning to vapes in the first place.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, I hope that the Government could work to strengthen mental health support interventions, especially amongst children, to be much more accessible and age-appropriate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even as we work to address vapes, we must also continue to play close attention to another societal health risk – smoking.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The increased enforcement against vapes might inadvertently cause users, especially those who use it as a means to quit smoking, to shift back to cigarettes for their nicotine fix.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Instead of viewing it as merely a sin tax, another revenue stream, I hope that the Government would explore more ways to use tobacco duties as a tool to tackle the negative externalities brought about by smoking to smokers, their loved ones and society at large.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The health implications of smoking are well known.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For smokers, these include the increased risk of cancer, heart disease and stroke.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Their loved ones, who would likely be subjected to second-hand smoke, would experience an increased cancer and stroke risk.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Meanwhile, people walking past smokers or the neighbours of smokers would likely be exposed to second-hand smoke and their associated risks while society at large would have to partially bear the cost of treating smoking-related health issues.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This has grave implications for our public health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The effect of nicotine on young brains, especially those under 25, are even more pronounced, given they are still not fully developed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is why banning smoking for those aged 21 and below may simply not be enough.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While the Government might write fully point out that New Zealand scrapped the ban in 2023, it was done so to subsidise tax cuts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, although the country has legalised vapes as a tobacco cessation device, thus leading smokers to turn to vapes instead, targeting the tobacco cohort ban at people born after a certain year, when they are still young children, will significantly minimise the exposure to both tobacco and vapes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Nevertheless, I believe that we can and should do more.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, our law should aim to rehabilitate and integrate rather than ostracise and stigmatise to curb smoking and vaping all together whilst preventing damages to lives and livelihoods.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is timely, it is forward looking and it recognises a very simple reality – that the threat simply has changed.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: What we are dealing with today is not just cigarettes in the traditional sense.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is also vaporisers, lookalike products and substances that can be mixed, disguised and marketed at speed, especially online.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And the people most at risk are our young.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: My remarks would be phased in three parts: first, on prevention and youth protection; second, the balance between enforcement and rehabilitation; and third, ground implementation so that the law is workable, fair and consistent.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If we want to protect young people, we have to act early, before harmful patterns become habits, before curiosity becomes dependency and before experimentation becomes identity.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is why I support the Bill's upstream preventive stance, especially provisions that deal with behavioural gateways and imitation products.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Because globally, we have seen how this plays out.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Products are designed to look harmless, even trendy.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Everything points to normalising the behaviour and then addiction becomes a problem.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But I want to ask about the "other half" of prevention.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Many young people do not start because they want to intentionally break the law.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: There is a lack of information, there is peer pressure and they tell themselves, "Well, it is just a vape." So, my first clarification is this.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Alongside enforcement, how the Ministry will ensure that there is preventive education and health literacy alongside and in a strong way?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: How will we then equip students and young people to recognise the risk early on?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: How will we support parents who may not even know	what to look out for and how to start conversations with their young ones?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: How will we keep our messaging current, when products evolve so quickly?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Because a strong preventive framework is not just regulation.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is also proactive, upstream education, delivered in a way that young people and their parents will actually receive and understand.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If I may offer one standard to guide us, the test is not how many rules we have, but how fewer young people are trapped in the first place.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It recognises rehabilitation as part of public health and that matters.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Because on the ground, we do see young offenders who are not hardened criminals.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But if we expand powers, we must also look to expand capacity.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, my second set of clarifications is about the scale and readiness.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Will there be an increase in training supervising officers?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Will counselling and psychosocial support services be expanded with these new pathways?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: How will community-based agencies be equipped to deliver effective rehabilitation programmes in a way that is structured, consistent and outcomes-oriented?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Otherwise, we create churn where the system looks busy, but the outcomes do not improve.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These are important measures, but many smaller premises may not have the experience managing regulatory responsibilities of this nature, so I want to seek clarification on what operational guidance will be provided.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Will there be practical tool kits, clear protocols, simple scripts for staff to use training for de-escalation so that they can comply with safety and be consistent about it?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We should not put our frontline workers in a position where they must enforce rules without the support, and then face confrontation without adequate protection.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In reality, an officer conducting a ground check may see a device, a liquid, a cartridge or a mixture.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Decisions would need to be made quickly, so I ask how will enforcement agencies operationally distinguish between these categories of devices and substances, especially when they are doing their ground checks and when they need to respond rapidly?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: First, it ensures proportional enforcement; and second, it can reduce confusion, both for the officers and the public.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If rules are clear, processes are fair and officers are supported, enforcement would become more consistent and confidence in the system would increase.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This Bill represents a careful and calibrated response to the growing public health challenge of vapes and smoking substances.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It tightens enforcement and it recognises for many, especially the young, early intervention and rehabilitation must be part of the process.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: With these remarks, Mr Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Renaming the act to the Tobacco and Vaporises Control Act 1993 rightly reflects a focus on modern delivery systems for nicotine and psychoactive substances.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I support the amendments in this Bill, which control the purchase, use, possession, import and supply of vaporisers and specified psychoactive substances.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, I would like to address in my speech the use of tobacco products in the form of smoking.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Smoking remains a primary driver of preventable disease and death in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These statistics represent thousands of families whose lives are upended by chronic illness, disability and premature death.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our objective should not be to merely regulate a harmful habit, but to systematically dismantle the structures that allow it to persist in our society through successive generations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Crucially, the Bill broadens the regulatory landscape by amending the long title to explicitly include the control of tobacco product use.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This transition from regulating commercial transactions to overseeing actual product usage provides a necessary legislative basis to address how these products impact the immediate environment of our residents.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The expansion of smoking bans in public places could have unintentionally pushed smokers into their homes to light up.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have received numerous complaints from my residents about smoke drifting into their homes from nearby units.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Currently, the authorities are only empowered to provide guidance to smokers to be more considerate.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In response to a Parliamentary Question on 10 September 2024, by my hon friend, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment said that the exhalation of cigarette smoke to the open air outside of the Housing and Development Board (HDB) flat is not a violation of the Smoking (Prohibition in Certain Places) regulations when the individual is smoking within the flat, as smoking is not prohibited in residential homes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While smoking within five metres of a of an HDB void deck is prohibited, smoking at home and blowing smoke in that same protected space is allowed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This highlights a gap in how we protect the air in and around our homes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Clause 37 of this Bill defines smoking as both inhaling and expelling of tobacco smoke.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Beyond residential smoking issues, we must move beyond managing the prevalence of smoking and start legislating for its eventual elimination for future generations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I reiterate my call from 5 March 2024 and echo my hon friend, Ms He Ting Ru, regarding a cohort tobacco ban.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This would make it illegal to sell tobacco products to or for them to be used by anyone born after a specific year.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I hope we can move forward on this expeditiously.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In fact, a crackdown on vaping without equally aggressive cigarette controls risk inadvertently pushing our youths towards smoking.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We would not want this Bill, which curbs vaping, to cause a resurgence in cigarette smoking by young people.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, anti-vaping strategies, which I support, must be structurally linked to a definitive tobacco phase out.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Next, we must examine the chemical composition of tobacco products on the market.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Nicotine is the primary driver of smoking addiction, and by restricting its concentration, we can reduce the pharmacological hook that makes it so difficult to quit using these products.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Under clause 6 of the Bill, which introduces the new section 14, the Minister is granted the power to set maximum allowable amounts for substances within tobacco products or their emissions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can I ask the Senior Minister of State what nicotine yield limit he intends to prescribe for this for Singapore under the new section 14?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Even in non-prohibited outdoor areas, a smoker walking ahead of a crowd creates a smoke trail that everyone behind is forced to inhale.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This requires greater public education and clearer guidelines on pedestrian etiquette and social responsibility.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In summary, Mr Speaker, while this Bill provides the necessary tools to control vaporisers and psychoactive substances, we must take this opportunity to protect residents from second-hand smoke.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must pair enforcement with a tobacco cohort ban to meaningfully reduce our national disease burden.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By addressing gaps in residential smoking and committing to a clear end game for tobacco, we can better safeguard the health of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is no longer a debate about lifestyle.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Devices that resemble vaporisers are now being used to deliver psychoactive substances.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What is marketed to youths as flavour and novelty can conceal sedation, dependency and real harm.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When a device can fit in a pocket yet deliver chemical dependence, the state must respond clearly and decisively.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I rise in strong support of the Bill.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, I support the move to future-proof our legislation.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If we regulate only what we already know, we will always be one step behind what arrives next.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If enforcement is reactive, exploitation will be proactive.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This architecture signals that Singapore intends to stay ahead of the curve, not chase it.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Second, deterrence must be sharpest where harm is multiplied.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Young users are visible, but organised importers and distributors are the engines of this problem.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The law must be firmest where profit meets exploitation.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must anticipate concealment methods, storage networks and cross-border sourcing.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would welcome the Senior Minister of State’s clarification on how agencies will prioritise dismantling organised supply networks and measure disruption of these channels, so that enforcement impact is visible and sustained.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the same time, deterrence alone cannot be the entire answer.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The credibility of this framework will depend on timely and consistent implementation.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For eligible first-time youth offenders, intervention must be swift, structured and supported by access to cessation and counselling pathways.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would be grateful if the Minister could elaborate on how agencies will ensure that diversion to rehabilitation is operationalised quickly, so that intervention is meaningful rather than delayed.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Chairman, protecting youths is not just a matter of law enforcement; it is the responsibility of our entire society.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Vaporisers today are no longer just nicotine products.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some have even become carriers of psychoactive substances.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If a small device can subtly alter a young person's mind, we cannot afford to be complacent.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must come down hard on those who supply these products for profit.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But we must also promptly intervene to help young people who have gone astray.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Strict measures are to cut off the source.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Tengah, I often hear young parents say that their biggest worry is not fines, but whether their children, out of momentary curiosity, will embark on a path of no return.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Bill is not simply a tobacco control measure.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It concerns the health of the next generation, the peace of mind of families and the bottom line of society.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Protecting youths is a principle we cannot compromise on.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, law alone does not shape norms.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A law is strongest when ordinary people understand it and can comply without fear or ambiguity.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As duties are placed on premises owners and responsible persons, guidance must be clear and practical.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Frontline staff must know what steps to take if they encounter suspected use or storage.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Enforcement communications must reinforce that detection is real and consequences are certain.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A firm law, consistently enforced, shapes behaviour long before it punishes it.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore has always taken a clear stance against substances that undermine public health and social stability.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In confronting the evolution of vaporisers into vehicles for psychoactive substances, we must be equally resolute.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Because ultimately, this Bill is not about devices.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The measure of a society is how firmly it protects its young, especially when the threat evolves.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: As the vapes or vaporisers are posing health hazards to our population, especially the youths and our students, I would like to seek answers to the following specific questions.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Number two: what are the educational and awareness programmes for students going forward?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Is it compulsory for students to attend such programmes and learn what are vapes and how bad it is?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Question three: is there any plan to equip or provide parents with tools for them to identify vaping devices and the potential use or identify the potential use of vapes by the child?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: My last question: the campus and the hostels of the institutes of higher learning (IHLs) are really porous and do we have plans to install vapes detection systems in the IHL campus and hostels?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 2.10 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 1.50 pm until 2.10 pm.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It did not resemble anything like a cigarette.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It did not resemble an item where many parents would traditionally associate with drugs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When he asked his daughter about it, she replied, "It's not like smoking.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It's not a drug." Sir, that moment illustrates how quickly substance misuse is evolving, how often, faster than public perception and regulation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We have clear prohibitions on the import, sale, possession and use of vaporisers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Yet what has evolved is not merely the device but the chemistry behind it.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, products are modified to include nicotine analogues.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, I will focus on the implementation because the strength of this Bill will ultimately depend on how it is operationalised.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: While my opening example involved a young person, we must be clear – this is not merely a youth issue.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The importation and distribution of Part 3A products containing specified psychoactive substances represent deliberate, profit-driven activities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The enhanced presumptions relating to possession and control are also important enforcement tools.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, I would like to seek clarification on how enforcement agencies intend to operationalise these strengthened provisions in increasingly complex supply environments, including decentralised storage and informal distribution channels.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Continuous monitoring and intelligence coordination will be essential.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To this end, the Bill equips authorised officers with the necessary powers to operate safely in enforcement situations that may involve risk.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I also note that the Bill strengthens operational powers under section 23B, including the use of restraints where necessary.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This recognises that enforcements against organised supply networks is not an administrative work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And for residents on the ground, this Bill sends a clear signal.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It tells parents that the law is keeping pace with substances designed to evade regulation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It tells communities that those who profit from distributing these products will face serious consequences.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And it reassures residents that enforcement agencies are being equipped with the powers needed to respond to new and evolving threats.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But as we strengthen enforcement and potentially increase the number of persons subject to rehabilitation orders, we must ensure there is an adequate capacity.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If rehabilitation becomes primarily supervisory without sufficient therapeutic intervention, we risk short-term compliance without that long-term recovery.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Substance misuse is not only a legal issue.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is also a behavioural and health issue.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Part 3B places duties on the responsible persons of specified premises.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is a significant shift towards shared responsibility.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It signals that enforcement cannot rest solely on the state.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, commercial storage operators, landlords, transport providers and small business owners will understandably seek clarity on what constitutes "due care" and "reasonable knowledge".

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Under the new section 18A, an owner or occupier commits an offence if they allow the storage of these prohibited items unless they have exercised "due care".

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For a small warehouse operator or a landlord, the difference between compliance and a heavy fine lie in the definition of that effort.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, we must ensure our business communities are not penalised for syndicates' sophisticated concealment tactics.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I welcome the indication that best-practice guidance may be developed.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, landlords, small shop operators or those managing shared premises may ask what constitutes reasonable steps to ensure that prohibited products are not stored on their premises.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As we strengthen enforcement against those distributing these substances, it will be important that guidance is clear so that law-abiding residents and businesses understand what is expected of them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To me, family involvement is critical, it is critical to sustain recovery and I support this principle.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: At the same time, we should ensure that such measures strengthen families rather than create adversarial dynamics.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Will there be flexibility for families facing financial or caregiving constraints?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If we require parental participation, we should also equip parents with knowledge and the practical tools to navigate.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Such a review could assess our enforcement outcomes, rehabilitation effectiveness, emerging substances' trends and operational challenges faced by responsible persons.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This would future-proof us, because future-proofing requires periodic recalibration.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What changed was the product's sophistication and the intent behind those distributing it.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It closes regulatory gaps, strengthens enforcement and provides the necessary tools to address substances designed to evade existing frameworks.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: We have been witnessing the rise of a new public health threat, that of vapes and its variants, especially those laced with dangerous chemicals, such as etomidate.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill will play an important role in addressing this threat.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: And we must act quickly, especially as the lives of many are being upended by the harmful nature of vaping.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: As we have all heard, vapes are highly addictive, often more so than traditional cigarettes.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Our youths have been particularly susceptible, as peddlers of vapes prey on those who are impressionable.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: The high concentrations of nicotine can trigger rapid brain responses, leading to quick dependency.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: And once hooked, trying to stop will provoke intense cravings and withdrawal.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: This was intended to be an interim measure, and it has given our authorities more power to prosecute importers, sellers or distributers of etomidate e-vaporisers under the MDA and mete out heavier penalties.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: As for consumers of these products, individuals found using etomidate e-vaporisers or who test positive for etomidate are not simply subjected to a fine, but have to undergo rehabilitation, treatment, mandatory supervision and even detention.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: But we now need to boost our laws to provide a more enduring framework to tackle vaping, and this Bill does that.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: First of all, I support the provisions of this Bill that would, in essence, treat the use of vapes with psychoactive substances in a way that is consistent with how we approach controlled drugs.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: It will also provide for testing methods to uncover consumption.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: As for users of vapes, in addition to stiffer fines, there are statutory rehabilitation programmes for users of psychoactive substances and this reflects a very calibrated response, with traffickers and sellers attracting strong punitive action, whereas the approach with vape users has a strong rehabilitative purpose which aims to help people break the addiction, work on their recovery and rehabilitate them back into society.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: I agree that this is a sound approach.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: While all offenders have to ultimately be accountable for their mistakes, we must also do our best to support them by providing available help to give them the best chance of quitting an addiction.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: I do have questions relating to how the Ministry hopes to achieve its rehabilitative objective.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: While community-based rehabilitation is an available pathway for users of vapes with psychoactive substances, for regular vape users, they will primarily be faced with a fine.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: And based on current policy, counselling programmes are mandatory for second-time offenders using regular vapes, but there is not much information available on what type of counselling programme will be made available to them and what other form of support will be provided particularly to students with vape addictions.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: I would therefore like to seek clarification from the Senior Minister of State, in the case of youths in schools who are discovered to be regular vape users, will there be any close collaboration or coordination with parents and schools to implement a structured programme or protocol to help them kick the habit?

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: While the addiction itself can wreck havoc on the student's ability to learn and concentrate in school, I can only imagine that as they go through withdrawal from nicotine and other addictive substances, this could have an equally deleterious effect, especially in the short term, and during particularly stressful periods like exams.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: It is hard enough for adults to quit, are we expecting fines and warnings or counselling alone to be sufficient to help school-going children and youths do so?

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: As for schools, I would argue that without professional guidance and support being offered, they, too, would be left to navigate these issues on their own.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, if we are going to do that, we should extend it to other forms of addiction amongst school-going kids, like gaming or even pornography.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, I would like to ask the Senior Minister of State if the Ministry intends to track the data of young vape users who are minors, to ensure that nicotine and other addictions are adequately identified and addressed?

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: This is similar to the point made by the hon Member Mr Yip.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: And lastly, will there be other steps taken to ensure that recidivism amongst youth vape users remains low?

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: That said, I support the Bill and look forward to the Senior Minister of State's clarifications.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I had spoken up in July last year on the etomidate situation and advocated for its classification under the MDA, because of what I felt were limitations under the existing framework of legislation at the time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It allowed tougher measures to be taken against those that trafficked etomidate and also permitted mandatory treatment to be ordered against abusers who would often refuse to attend treatment voluntarily.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This last point is reinforced by Senior Minister of State Koh's point in his introductory speech, that the number of abusers defaulted even on mandatory treatment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I was initially a little concerned about whether this meant we were taking a lighter touch approach against etomidate, but looking at the penalties involved, it appears the regime is largely similar to that used in relation to Class C drugs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think Senior Minister of State Koh also confirmed this in his introductory speech.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This suggests we are not taking a lighter touch approach against etomidate, and to the extent, this reclassification is administrative, to put it on a longer term footing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of the strengths of this Bill is the flexibility it confers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This allows the Government to stay ahead of synthetic variants which are engineered specifically to exploit gaps in the legal framework.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is especially useful because so-called "designer drugs" can proliferate because of delays in the implementation of statutory control.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In comparison, under the MDA, a psychoactive substance is defined in section 2 conceptually to mean "a substance or product that has the capacity to have a psychoactive effect on an individual if the individual smokes, administers to himself or herself or otherwise consumes, the substance or product" and which is not an "excluded substance" under the Fifth Schedule.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Part 2A of the MDA contains provisions dealing with psychoactive substances generally and can be a conceptual catch-all mechanism for drugs that are not classified elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In contrast, those psychoactive substances that are already known are often classified as drugs and specific penalties would apply to those.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This essentially means there will be two statutes which could potentially deal with new psychoactive substances: one, they could be classified in the Schedule under this new Act; or two, they could still be captured conceptually under the MDA.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In relation to this, I make three points.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: First, in future, what considerations will determine whether a psychoactive substance is to be listed under the TVCA?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Second, is it possible for a case to be caught by both the TVCA and the MDA, and if so, how will the authorities decide which statute to prosecute an offender under?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Third, will sentencing guidelines and cases under the MDA apply to cases under the TVCA?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In my view, certainly, etomidate-related cases should apply.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is largely misused through vaporisers and related products and that may be the reason for its classification under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, the potential for vaporisers to administer more serious drugs has always been present, and the infamous Kpod was known to contain either etomidate or ketamine.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Ketamine is, of course, classified as a drug under the MDA.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While I understand the rationale for placing etomidate under this Bill and therefore the jurisdiction of HSA, what happens if more harmful substances or drugs are found while the HSA is conducting a raid for vaporisers and/or etomidate?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Would HSA be empowered to effect arrests and take enforcement actions, assuming drugs are also found with the vaporisers?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In contrast, I understand the Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) officers have much broader powers of arrest.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I believe the HSA will need to adequately resourced and empowered to discharge the new role.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Likewise, the CNB should continue to be empowered to effect arrests for etomidate in the event they come across this substance while effecting arrests or investigations into other drugs and psychoactive substances.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The rehabilitation aspect of the Bill is also important.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The framework allows for community-based rehabilitation and institutional treatment where appropriate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This mirrors, in many respects, the approach taken under the MDA.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It recognises that while enforcement and deterrence are essential, rehabilitation remains a cornerstone of our drug control policy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, here again, there appears to be a potential overlap between the two statutes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would be grateful if the Ministry would clarify two points.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: First, would offenders subject to mandatory treatment under this Bill be sent to DRCs currently used for drug offenders or is the intention to send them to different facilities?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If there are to be different facilities, the HSA will need the resources to set up such centres.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We must continue to emphasise prevention, education and parental involvement.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We must not be seen to compromise on this when new substances emerge.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Members have raised a number of thoughtful views and constructive comments.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I have touched on some of these in my opening speech, so I will now elaborate more on other areas that were raised by Members.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: First, beyond increasing penalties to enhance deterrence, Mr Yip Hon Weng asked whether our enforcement approach would truly reduce youth exposure and initiation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Well, the fact is that firm enforcement alone will never eliminate vaping.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: However, a strong deterrence posture remains essential if we are serious about reducing the harm it can cause to our people.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Vaping has not yet become deeply entrenched in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This gives us a critical window to act decisively.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That is why we are targeting the entire supply ecosystem, the entire supply chain, through robust enforcement while at the same time supporting users through rehabilitation to prevent vaping from taking root in our society.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Dr Hamid Razak and Mr Vikram Nair rightly pointed out the importance of preventive education.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Many people, especially the young, picked up vaping out of curiosity or peer pressure.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Therefore, we have also stepped up preventive education efforts in tandem.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The national campaign across multiple platforms includes digital display panels cross the island, in our heartlands, especially, mainstream media and social media to inform the public about the dangers of vaping and etomidate vaporisers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We also collaborated with many online content partners to reach out to young people because this is where young people are consuming information, so this is a good way to reach out to them.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Schools and IHLs have also played a big part to educate the young on the harm and consequences of vaping.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The messages are also integrated into the school curriculum.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Dr Neo Kok Beng asked about this earlier.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For those who have already started vaping, we adopted a calibrated multi-layered approach.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This approach provides multiple chances to quit before the more serious penalties apply.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: First, the avenue to seek help to quit remains open under the QuitVape Programme.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Those who come forward voluntarily will not be penalised for doing so.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Next, for individuals who have been caught vaping, penalties will kick in, along with a requirement to attend rehabilitation for repeat offenders.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For those consuming etomidate, testing of their urine or hair samples may be required on top of rehabilitation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To Ms Kuah Boon Theng's question, students caught for the first time will be guided by school counsellors and referred to the Health Promotion Board's (HPB's) QuitLine when needed.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Her suggestion of working in a more coordinated manner across different Ministries, resourcing the counsellors, is something that we will take back and look at how to do so, although today, we do have close collaboration between HSA and the Ministry of Education.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To Dr Choo Pei Ling's question, suspected offenders may have to undergo interviews, investigations and testing prior to being sent for rehabilitation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This explains the turnaround time between detection and start of the rehabilitation programme.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We are working to minimise this turnaround time.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The providers of rehabilitation programmes will explore the underlying causes for the use of vaporisers and etomidate, and offenders will learn healthy coping habits and how to withstand peer pressure.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These are tips that will help them to sustain a vaporiser-free lifestyle, post rehabilitation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For youths under 21 years old, the Youth Enhanced Supervision Scheme under the Ministry of Social and Family Development has an added element of family involvement, with some sessions conducted together with their parents or guardians.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Parents can also refer to the Parent's Guide on Vaping on the Families for Life website for tips on having conversations with their children on vaping.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To Dr Wan Rizal's question, HSA will closely engage parents and guardians and use the powers of section 19S judiciously.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Parental and family support, I am sure we all agree, are crucial to helping young offenders quit.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Parents who refuse to be involved in their children's counselling without reasonable justifications will potentially face criminal charges.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: However, despite our best efforts, if individuals decide to re-offend repeatedly, penalties will escalate rapidly.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In answer to Mr Vikram Nair's question, this will be separate from other drug offenders.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: By the time they are sent to the DRC, these reoffenders would have been caught at least three times and given multiple chances to quit.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We have to go really upstream and stop the flow of these items into Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If the products contain SPS, the penalties will be as severe and aligned to those for Class C controlled drugs under the MDA.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: During the investigations of suspected import and supply offences, HSA takes into account several factors, including the quantity and types of prohibited products involved as well as evidence of intent to sell or supply to others, to determine the nature of the offence and how an individual is involved.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Factors such as age and number of past offences will be taken into consideration by the Courts when determining the appropriate sentences.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Specifically for youth offenders, the Courts will also consider youth-specific sentencing options such as probation or reformative training.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As Mr Yip and Dr Wan Rizal mentioned, supply channels are becoming more complex and decentralised, especially through the use of social media and messaging platforms.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On the ground, we have also adapted our enforcement approach to better detect import and supply offences.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: First, HSA actively monitors sales and advertisements of vaporisers on such platforms and works with platform owners to remove these listings.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: HSA also collaborates with the Infocomm Media Development Authority and the Online Criminal Harms Act (OCHA) Office to block vaporiser websites targeting locals.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA), CNB and Singapore Police Force already engage in information sharing with their foreign counterparts.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will work closely to make sure that we have intelligence to deal with this.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Dr Hamid, Mr Yip, Dr Wan Rizal, Dr Choo and Mr Vikram Nair have raised a few operational issues.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Members asked how enforcement actions will be differentiated for SPS under the TVCA, and controlled drugs and psychoactive substances under the MDA.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: A SPS, once scheduled under the TVCA, will be automatically excluded from the framework of psychoactive substances under the MDA because this framework in MDA works on a negative list approach and SPS has been excluded.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To Dr Hamid and Mr Yip's question on frontline enforcement, officers will assess the situation to route the case to the appropriate agency.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Laboratory testing of the substance may be conducted to ascertain the identity of the substances involved and subsequently refer to the appropriate authorities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To Mr Vikram Nair's questions, when it comes to rehabilitation, those who are suspected or are found to have consumed only SPS will be handled by HSA.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If both SPS and controlled drugs or psychoactive substances under the MDA are consumed, the MDA rehabilitation framework will take precedence, given the seriousness of those drugs and offences.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: HSA and CNB will investigate the cases jointly if necessary.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The ultimate decision on prosecution will be made by the Attorney-General's Chambers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For cases to be charged under the TVCA, we will take guidance from the existing body of law, including precedent cases charged under the MDA.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Support will be provided to owners and occupiers of specified premises so they will understand how to fulfil their new obligations.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
